turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today? Patient: I’ve been dealing with severe itching of my vulva that’s been gradually getting worse over the past year, and it hasn’t improved much with over-the-counter lubricants. I also have painful intercourse, so I’ve stopped being sexually active because it hurts too much.
Doctor: Can you describe exactly when the itching started and whether it comes on suddenly or has been slowly increasing over the past year?

Patient: It started gradually about a year ago, and it’s been slowly getting worse rather than suddenly coming on. The itching tends to be pretty constant, but it can flare and feel most intense at certain times during the day.
Doctor: May I ask how old you are and whether you’re currently going through menopause or have had any changes in your menstrual cycle?

Patient: I’m 60 years old, and I went through menopause around age 52, so I haven’t had menstrual changes since then. The itching and discomfort have been increasing over the last year even though I’m postmenopausal.
Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in the appearance of the skin on your vulva—such as redness, white or gray patches, thinning, fissures, bumps, or any sores?

Patient: The skin looks a bit irritated and red at times, and I’ve noticed some thinning and small cracks or fissures. I haven’t really seen any obvious sores, but there are occasional bumps and the area looks different than it used to.
Doctor: Do you ever notice any vaginal discharge, odor, or a feeling of wetness, and if so, what color or consistency is it?

Patient: I don’t really notice any unusual discharge, odor, or a wet feeling—no distinct color or consistency change. It’s mostly constant vulvar itching with the irritation and the small cracks, and that’s been driving the discomfort.

Doctor: Have you started using any new soaps, bubble baths, laundry detergents, feminine wipes, or topical creams (including over‑the‑counter moisturizers or lubricants) in the past year that might come into contact with the vulvar skin?

Patient: I haven’t used any new soaps or bubble baths, but I did try several over-the-counter lubricants and moisturizers, and neither helped much. I also haven’t used any feminine wipes or prescription creams, just the usual hygiene products I’ve been using for a while.
Doctor: Do you experience any pain, burning, or urgency when you urinate, or any bleeding or spotting after urination?

Patient: I don’t have any burning or urgency when I urinate, and I haven’t noticed any bleeding or spotting after urination. It’s mainly the vulvar itching with irritation and the cracking that makes things uncomfortable.
Doctor: Have you noticed any white

Patient: I haven’t really noticed any specific white or gray patches, but the area does look more irritated at times, with thinning and small cracks. Sometimes there are a few bumps, and the skin just seems different than it used to. The main issue is the severe itching and the pain with intercourse.
Doctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with any skin conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, or lichen planus elsewhere on your body, or do you have a personal or family history of autoimmune diseases?

Patient: I haven’t been diagnosed with psoriasis, eczema, or lichen planus anywhere else, and I don’t really have a known personal or family history of autoimmune diseases. I do have diet-controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension, but no other skin or immune conditions that I’m aware of.
Doctor: Have you ever tried or are you currently using any topical estrogen or hormonal creams in the genital area, or have you been on systemic hormone therapy since menopause?

Patient: I haven’t used any topical estrogen or hormonal creams in the genital area, and I haven’t taken systemic hormone therapy since menopause. I’ve mainly just tried over-the-counter lubricants and moisturizers, but they didn’t give me much relief.

Doctor: When you look at the affected area, do you see any smooth, white, shiny patches that feel a bit like parchment or paper—often described as “white plaques”—or does the skin look more red and raw without those white spots?

Patient: I don’t see clear smooth white shiny “plaques” like you described, but the area is often red and irritated. I do notice thinning and small cracks/fissures, and sometimes a few bumps, and it’s mainly the severe itching that’s getting worse.
[DDX] Lichen sclerosus, Lichen planus, Atrophic vulvovaginitis (genitourinary syndrome of menopause), Contact dermatitis, Chronic vulvar eczema
